title: Span, unsafe code, and interop — interview

items.question: Why can you not store Span<T> on a class or await with one live?
items.answer: Span<T> is a ref struct. It may point at stack memory or a slice of an array. The compiler forbids putting it on the heap (class fields, async state machines, iterators across yield) so a stack frame cannot disappear under it. Use Memory<T> when the buffer must survive an await, then .Span only in synchronous sections.
followUps: What did C# 13 change for ref locals in async methods?
What did C# 14 add for spans?
items.sixtySeconds: ref struct, no heap. Memory for async. C# 14 implicit conversions. C# 13: scoped span across more APIs.

items.question: How would you parse a large CSV without a string per cell?
items.answer: Keep the line as ReadOnlySpan<char> (or bytes). IndexOf the delimiter, Slice the cell, parse ints with int.TryParse on the span. stackalloc a scratch buffer for a decoded row if the line is bounded. Do not Substring unless you must retain the value after the buffer is reused.
followUps: When is stackalloc the wrong tool?
items.sixtySeconds: Slice, don't Substring. TryParse on span. stackalloc only for small bounded scratch.

items.question: What does fixed do, and when do you still need unsafe?
items.answer: fixed pins a managed object so the GC cannot relocate it, giving a pointer valid inside the statement. unsafe is the context that allows pointer types. Prefer Span and MemoryMarshal over raw pointers. You need unsafe for function pointers, pointer arithmetic, or some P/Invoke signatures — not for ordinary slicing.
followUps: Can you fixed a span across a p/invoke without a length?
items.sixtySeconds: fixed pins. unsafe enables pointers. Span first. Never pass a span pointer as a C string without length.

items.question: How should a C# engineer talk about P/Invoke in an interview?
items.answer: It is a marshalling boundary: calling convention, character set, ownership of native memory, and lifetime. Prefer LibraryImport source generation over DllImport. Wrap native handles in IDisposable (SkiaSharp lesson). This is not an invitation to rewrite the worker in C++.
followUps: Span vs Memory when wrapping native calls?
items.sixtySeconds: Boundary, not a C++ course. LibraryImport. Dispose native. Span sync, Memory async.
